8 अगस्त के लिए मौसम का पूर्वानुमान: उत्तर में स्थानीय लू, दक्षिण में छिटपुट बारिश।
8 अगस्त, 2026 के लिए मौसम पूर्वानुमान: उत्तरी वियतनाम में वर्षा तेजी से कम होगी और स्थानीय लू चलने लगेगी। मध्य वियतनाम में छिटपुट बौछारें और गरज के साथ बारिश जारी रहेगी, जबकि दक्षिणी वियतनाम में दोपहर और शाम के समय स्थानीय स्तर पर भारी बारिश होती रहेगी।
VietNamNet•07/08/2026
राष्ट्रीय जल-मौसम विज्ञान पूर्वानुमान केंद्र के अनुसार, उत्तरी और मध्य क्षेत्रों में गरज-चमक वाले तूफान तेजी से कम हो रहे हैं। 8 अगस्त को, उत्तरी क्षेत्र में केवल कुछ स्थानों पर ही गरज-चमक वाले तूफान आएंगे; दिन में धूप खिली रहेगी, हालांकि कुछ क्षेत्रों में स्थानीय लू चलने की संभावना है, जहां अधिकतम तापमान 35 डिग्री सेल्सियस से अधिक हो सकता है।
गौरतलब है कि 9 अगस्त से वियतनाम के उत्तरपूर्वी क्षेत्र में व्यापक लू चलने की संभावना है।
विशेष रूप से, 7 अगस्त को हनोई में मौसम धूप वाला और शुष्क हो गया, तापमान तेजी से बढ़कर लगभग 35 डिग्री सेल्सियस के अधिकतम स्तर तक पहुंच गया, जिससे काफी गर्मी और उमस महसूस हुई।
इसके अतिरिक्त, थान्ह होआ से ह्यू शहर और दक्षिण मध्य तटीय क्षेत्र तक के इलाके में शाम और रात में छिटपुट बारिश और गरज के साथ बौछारें पड़ेंगी; दिन में धूप खिली रहेगी, कुछ इलाकों में गर्मी रहेगी; विशेष रूप से, थान्ह होआ से उत्तरी क्वांग त्रि तक के इलाके में छिटपुट बारिश और गरज के साथ बौछारें पड़ेंगी।
मध्य और दक्षिणी हाइलैंड्स में दिन के दौरान धूप रहेगी, दोपहर और शाम के बाद छिटपुट बौछारें और गरज के साथ बारिश होगी, और कुछ क्षेत्रों में स्थानीय रूप से भारी बारिश होगी।
मौसम विज्ञान एजेंसी का कहना है कि गरज के साथ आने वाले तूफान बवंडर, बिजली, ओले और तेज हवाओं का कारण बन सकते हैं। भारी बारिश से निचले इलाकों में तेजी से बाढ़ आ सकती है; छोटी नदियों और नालों में अचानक बाढ़ आ सकती है और ढलानों पर भूस्खलन हो सकता है।

Fourth regional heat wave ends in Limburg as weekend temps set to climb above 30°C
A fourth regional heat wave was recorded in the southern Netherlands this year, ending Friday after lasting a week and a half. In the meantime, the weekend is expected to turn hot nationwide, with temperatures rising above 30 degrees Celsius in many places on Sunday. The next heatwave might also start some time soon, Weeronline forecasts.
A maximum temperature of 24.1 degrees in Maastricht on Friday brought the regional heat wave in the south to a close. The heat wave in Limburg began July 28, when temperatures first exceeded 25 degrees, and remained above that mark for 10 consecutive days until Friday.
Another regional heat wave is expected soon. After a brief cooler period, temperatures will climb this weekend. Friday’s highs ranged from 21 to locally 25 degrees, levels normal for this time of year.
A heat wave is defined as five consecutive days above 25 degrees Celsius, including at least three days above 30 degrees. Ell, Limburg, was the first place to meet those criteria on Aug. 1, followed by Maastricht on Aug. 2.”
Saturday will feature abundant sunshine with at most some high cloud cover. Highs are forecast to reach 25 degrees in the northwest and 28 degrees in the southeast, with light winds creating pleasant conditions for outdoor activities. Overnight lows of 13 to 16 degrees will allow for the country to cool down a little.
Sunday will be hotter. Large parts of the country are expected to see tropical temperatures of 30 to 32 degrees. Coastal areas will be milder at 26 to 29 degrees.
A weak to moderate southwesterly wind will offer extra cooling along the coast. Sunshine will be plentiful and conditions dry.
After the weekend, temperatures will ease temporarily before rising again later in the week, when a return of tropical readings is expected.
The sunny, warm pattern will further increase the drought, affecting shipping and agriculture. Several water boards have been urging residents to use water sparingly.

Hong Kong temperatures exceed 38 degrees as Severe Typhoon Dolphin brings extreme heat
Forecaster says extremely hot weather is expected to continue into early next week
Temperatures exceeded 38 degrees Celsius (100 Fahrenheit) in parts of Hong Kong on Saturday as the city’s forecaster warned that extremely hot weather would persist over the coming days.
The Hong Kong Observatory said Severe Typhoon Dolphin was bringing high temperatures to the region, with the heat expected to continue into early next week.
“With [Severe Typhoon] Dolphin moving towards the vicinity of Zhejiang and northern Fujian, its outer subsiding air will persistently bring extremely hot weather to the area in the next couple of days,” the Observatory said.
A very hot weather warning was issued at 6.45am, while the Labour Department issued an amber heat stress at work warning about 15 minutes later.
The temperature reached 34.1 degrees at the Observatory’s headquarters in Tsim Sha Tsui at around 1.30pm. Elsewhere, temperatures climbed well above 35 degrees in the afternoon.

Dakota Gardener: Helping gardens survive extreme heat
Yikes! It is hot – dangerously hot. Our plants in the garden are wilting, and we are soaked in sweat trying to care for them.
My cucumber and zucchini vines droop every afternoon. The initial harvest was great, but production is slowing down due to the extreme heat. The vines are producing fewer female (fruit-bearing) flowers. The pollen from the male flowers is less effective in this heat, too.
Bees don’t like this scorching heat. They are seeking shade and becoming less active pollinating our crops.
The combination of fewer female flowers, poor pollen and reduced bee activity will lead to a short-term reduction in production. I expect some of my next flush of cucumbers will be curled and misshapen because of insufficient pollination.
Our tomatoes are suffering. When temperatures exceed 85 degrees Fahrenheit daily, tomato flowers may wither before setting fruits. Tomato fruits on the vine will be slower to redden and ripen.
We expect an uptick in more tomato fruits suffering from blossom end rot. This rot at the bottom of fruits is caused by a lack of calcium. Hot, dry conditions reduce soil moisture. When soil moisture is low, less calcium flows from the soil into the fruits, causing more blossom end rot.
Many peppers are getting sunburned. These scalded fruits are found on smaller plants that lack the foliage to shade the fruits.
One way to combat excessive heat is to shade our plants. Shade cloth can be hung over them. Container plants can be moved to shady areas.
Adding mulch will conserve soil moisture. Be sure the mulch, whether it be straw or grass clippings, was not treated with herbicide.
Most of us respond to our wilting plants by irrigating them. Let’s discuss the proper way to irrigate your plants.
First, it is better to irrigate deeply and infrequently rather than giving your plants a sip of water every day. Roots grow where the water is. If you irrigate deeply, the roots of the plants will grow deeply. That’s what we want.
Next, irrigate in the morning after sunrise. Plants in the morning absorb the water they need, and their leaves will dry quickly. Avoid mid-day irrigation because you will lose much of the water from evaporation. Avoid watering at night because prolonged periods of wet leaves will lead to disease.
Do not use overhead irrigation. Why do we irrigate the leaves of a plant? A plant drinks primarily through its roots, not leaves. We should irrigate the roots. Wet leaves lead to disease.
This reminds me of my first job: a sunflower killer at Northrup King Seed Company. The scientists at the company trained me to kill as many sunflower plants as possible with diseases. The goal was to discover a disease-resistant variety that I could not kill.
I grew diseases in the laboratory during the day and then sprinkled the disease spores on the plants at night. Then I turned on the overhead sprinklers. The presence of diseases along with wet leaves at night was a deadly combination.
This deadly combination continues to work today. There is a huge outbreak of blight now on tomato and potato vines in my community garden. My fellow gardeners tell me this happens every year.
That’s because most of them wet the leaves of their plants when watering. Don’t do that! Instead, use a watering wand or soaker hose. Direct the water at the roots of the plants and keep the leaves dry.
Plants in our gardens are wilting today, but they can recover with your help. Irrigate early in the day, irrigate deeply and keep the leaves dry. Once this heat wave cools off, you may be rewarded with a bountiful harvest.
For more information about gardening, contact your local NDSU Extension agent.

Much of the Bay Area is set to see sizzling summer weather this weekend as temperatures hit the triple digits, but coastal areas will mostly avoid the swelter with much more temperate conditions.
Heat advisories go into effect Saturday at 10 a.m. and will remain in effect through Sunday at 10 p.m., said National Weather Service meteorologist Anamaria Nagarrete.
“More inland areas, particularly the interior valleys of the North Bay, East Bay and even South Bay as well as down on the Central Coast, can see temperatures as high as the mid-90s to the lower 100s,” Nagarrete said. “Once you get closer to the coast and right at the bay, we can see that marine influence holding on strong and moderating temperatures to the 70s, to even upper 60s.”
Friday’s weather ushered in some monsoonal moisture in upper clouds, but most of that was set to remain at higher elevations, Nagarrete said. Saturday and Sunday were likely to introduce moderate heat risks, which will begin to lower to a minor heat risk on Monday.
Nagarrete encouraged those who want to spend time outdoors over the weekend to take precautions due to the heat, including staying hydrated and drinking electrolytes, wearing sunscreen and other sun protection and limiting time spent outdoors. No children or pets should be left unattended in vehicles.
San Jose will see highs into the low to mid-90s on Saturday and Sunday, with lows dipping down to mid-to-low 60s, Nagarrete said. The heat risk in the South Bay is highest near San Jose, in the Santa Cruz Mountains and in the eastern Santa Clara Hills, according to the NWS.
In the East Bay, inland cities such as Livermore will spike to 96 on Saturday and up to 100 on Sunday, while more coastal Oakland will only heat up to the upper 70s and low 80s. Walnut Creek will see a high of 94 on Saturday and 101 on Sunday, with lows in the low 60s. The East Bay heat risk is highest in the region’s interior hills and valleys, according to NWS.
San Francisco will largely escape the swelter, with highs expected to hit 73 on Saturday and 77 on Sunday, with lows dipping into the upper 50s.
“The brunt of the force of that heat is going to be on Saturday and Sunday, and then beginning Monday, we should see a gradual cooldown,” Nagarrete added. “We still have a minor heat risk because … our high pressure system is holding on pretty strong over at the southwest and seems like it’s not going anywhere until probably the later half of the incoming work week.”
Bay Area residents traveling to the Lake Tahoe area for the weekend will not be able to escape the heat there, either. Temperatures are expected to peak in the lower 90s on Saturday and Sunday, but there is no heat advisory in place because temperatures will be dipping into the 50s overnight, said NWS meteorologist Mark Deutschendorf. Beginning Monday, there will be a “slow cooling trend” with highs dropping to the upper 80s and hitting the low 80s by the end of the week.
“It is on the hot side compared to their normals,” he said. “They normally would see lower 80s this time of year.”
“Between the Bay Area and Tahoe, it’ll be quite hot in the valleys, so that’s always something to keep an eye on,” he added. “The drive there will be pretty heated, so you should have a vehicle well maintained and carry extra water in the car with you.”
That heat combined with a low humidity of 10% to 40% is also bringing elevated fire weather conditions in the Bay Area, Nagarrete said. Fire weather advisories are in place for the North Bay and East Bay for Friday through Sunday, warning of elevated fire conditions with the potential for rapid spread of flames, according to NWS.
“This heat … is drying out the vegetation that we have at our higher elevation peaks, which are places that we’re monitoring for,” Nagarrete said. “It’s just making them more susceptible to burn if a fire were to be ignited, and that’s combined with lower relative humidity recoveries overnight.”
“The only thing that we’re lacking is the wind component,” she added.
Smoke impacts on the greater Bay Area from a fire burning in Sonoma County, which had lowered air quality earlier in the week, were “very limited” to none, Nagarrete said, adding that the fire has reached 95% containment.
The heat-up will be accompanied by a coastal flood advisory warning of flooding of up to 1.7 feet in low-lying coastal areas along the edges of San Francisco, San Pablo and Monterey bays, according to the NWS. The advisory was set to go into effect 5 p.m. Friday and last until 2 a.m. Thursday. The warning anticipated flooding in roads, parks and lots with isolated road impacts.
“That’s mainly due to the high tides that we are experiencing,” Nagarrete said.
Nagarrete added that Bay Area residents should plan for extra travel time if going near coastal areas and take steps to protect valuables on flood-prone properties. Some low-lying coastal trails and beaches may also have access blocked by high tide.
“Never drive through any barricades or through water, as people may underestimate just how deep that water is,” she added. “It’s just better to err on the side of caution and to not drive through any type of water.”
The NWS is also monitoring for a southerly swell of 15 to 17 seconds along the coast that was set to arrive Friday evening and last until Sunday, Nagarrete added. That has the potential to increase the risk of strong rip currents and sneaker waves.
“Our wave heights aren’t necessarily high enough for us to meet beach hazards criteria,” Nagarrete said. “But because it’s going to be so hot and I’m sure people would love to go and experience our beautiful coastline, we just always emphasize taking extra precautions whenever people are visiting the beaches because the ocean can be very unforgiving.”

OZARK, Ala. (WTVY) - As fall sports practices get underway, extreme heat is adding another challenge for athletes and coaches across the Wiregrass.
Football players are working through intense drills in helmets and pads, equipment that can make already high temperatures even more dangerous. Athletic trainer Lori Long says preparation — before athletes ever step on the field — is key to preventing heat illness.
“On the field, that’s usually too late to deal with heat injuries, heat exhaustion or heat illness,” Long said.
Long has worked as an athletic trainer for 18 years and previously spent 15 years as an active-duty combat medic. She said the demands of training in extreme heat can create similar concerns for athletes and soldiers.
Hydration starts before practice
Heat advisories do not necessarily stop practices, but trainers and coaches must adjust when temperatures climb, especially as players add pads, helmets and high-intensity workouts.
Long said an unusually hot July brought high temperatures earlier than usual. Her focus is on educating athletes to hydrate before they arrive at practice and to keep drinking water during team meetings and throughout the day.
At Carroll, Long and her staff meet with coaches daily to review the heat index and plan water and rest breaks. She said open communication is essential.
“That’s the most important thing, because in our job, we have to do a lot of convincing and letting them know we’re not trying to hold your kid out,” Long said. “We are their advocate.”
Cooling supplies ready on the sideline
Long’s team keeps water, ice towels and a cold-water immersion tub available for a serious heat emergency. She also uses a cooling technique she learned in the military: submerging an athlete’s arms or legs in cold water, up to the armpits, to help cool them quickly.
Still, she said the goal is to prevent athletes from reaching that point.
Trainers recommend athletes drink plenty of water throughout the day. Long said education also has to continue at home, where families can watch for unusual fatigue, changes in sleep patterns and nutrition concerns.
She said cramps and the risk of heat-related illness remain constant worries during the preseason, but prevention works best when athletes, families, coaches and trainers are all paying attention.
As teams prepare for Friday night football and the fall sports season, Long’s message is simple: Speak up if something does not feel right.
“Extreme heat can turn a normal practice into a dangerous situation quickly,” she said. “Prevention can make all the difference.”

The maximum temperature was 27.5 degrees Celsius, seven degrees below normal, against Thursday’s 27.6. The minimum temperature was 25.6 degrees Celsius, one degree below normal and the same as the previous day.
IMD’s data shows that heavy rainfall was seen mostly at stations in south and southwest Delhi. From 8.30am to 8pm, Pushp Vihar received the maximum rainfall at 147.5mm, followed by Chhatarpur at 131mm. Among the other stations that saw heavy rainfall are Aya Nagar at 87.4mm, Palam at 88.7mm, Jharoda Kalan at 69.5mm, Janakpuri at 72mm and Pusa at 67.5mm.
The Met department classifies rainfall as light when it is up to 15.5mm; as moderate, when it ranges from 15.6mm to 64.4mm, and as heavy, when it’s between 64.5 and 115.5mm in a 24-hour period.
Most areas saw moderate showers, with base station Safdarjung recording 77.1mm, Ridge in north Delhi 49.6mm and Lodhi Road 49.3mm between 8.30am and 5.30pm.
This Aug so far, Safdarjung has received 127mm of rainfall as opposed to the entire month’s normal of 233.1 mm. The city witnessed two heavy rainfall days in July. Though Delhi saw a rain deficit of 44% in June, July ended with a rain surplus of 23%.
The maximum temperature, which has now remained below 30 degrees Celsius for two days, is likely to remain between 30 and 32 degrees Celsius Saturday. “It is likely to be 33-35 degrees Celsius from Sunday. The minimum temperature is predicted to settle between 22 and 24 degrees Celsius over the next few days,” said a Met official.
Though there are chances of light-to-moderate rain Saturday, the city is likely to receive light-to-very light rain from Sunday to next Thursday.
The rain helped in keeping Delhi’s air quality index on the lower side by washing out pollutants. At 63, AQI remained satisfactory for the eighth consecutive day. It was 74 Thursday.

Kerala rains persist, schools shut in 8 districts, orange alert issued
Rains continued in several parts of Kerala on Saturday, prolonging waterlogging and inundation in many districts, while the IMD forecast moderate rainfall at isolated places in seven districts in the morning.
Moderate rainfall accompanied by winds reaching up to 30 kmph is very likely at isolated places in Thiruvananthapuram, Idukki, Ernakulam, Kozhikode, Wayanad, Kannur and Kasaragod districts, the India Meteorological Department said.
Light rainfall is likely at isolated places in the remaining districts, it said.
With floodwaters yet to recede completely, a large number of people continued to stay in relief camps in several south and central districts.
For Sunday, the IMD has issued an orange alert for Pathanamthitta, Alappuzha, Kottayam, Kozhikode, Wayanad, Kannur and Kasaragod districts.
An orange alert refers to very heavy rain of 11 cm to 20 cm.
The Upper Kuttanad and Kuttanad regions of Alappuzha remained inundated, though floodwaters were gradually receding, officials said.
In several coastal areas, high waves, sea incursion and strong winds kept fishermen off the sea.
In view of the prevailing rains, holidays have been declared for all educational institutions in eight districts — Kasaragod, Kannur, Wayanad, Kozhikode, Thrissur, Kottayam, Pathanamthitta and Alappuzha —for Saturday as a precautionary measure.
The holiday applies to all educational institutions, from anganwadis to professional colleges, authorities said.
The Kerala State Disaster Management Authority (KSDMA) said strong winds were among the state's most destructive weather-related hazards, often causing damage by uprooting trees and snapping branches.
It advised people not to take shelter under trees or park vehicles beneath them during strong winds and rain.
Residents were also advised to prune weak branches around their homes and report dangerous trees in public places to local authorities.
People were asked to keep doors and windows closed once strong winds begin, avoid standing near them and refrain from staying on terraces.
Those living in houses with thatched roofs, sheet roofing or other structurally weak buildings were advised to move to safer shelters or relief camps if directed by authorities.
Local self-government institutions, revenue officials and elected representatives have been asked to facilitate the evacuation of vulnerable residents to relief camps wherever necessary.
